title_de: Die Offense von Kyle Shanahan: Was ist das Besondere am Scheme? Teil 1
title_en: Kyle Shanahan’s offense: what makes the scheme special? Part 1
teaser_de: Bevor es um das Scheme selbst geht: Kyle Shanahans Weg durch den Coaching-Tree, vom Assistenten bis zum Head Coach der 49ers.
teaser_en: Before getting to the scheme itself: Kyle Shanahan’s path through the coaching tree, from assistant to 49ers head coach.
body_en:
## A look inside the modern NFL offense

## Introduction

Any fan of American football, and of the NFL in particular, who occasionally scrolls through the relevant social media platforms won't need long to find some post or tweet in which someone talks about the "**scheme**." On offense, this usually means that the quarterback got no help from the scheme and therefore played badly, or, if he had a statistically good or outstanding game, it gets explained away by saying the scheme did the work for him and his own share was rather small. You hear this especially often about quarterbacks who play in a system based on the ideas of Mike Shanahan. As explained in more detail later in this series, almost half of all teams now have offensive play-callers who came into contact with Mike Shanahan's system at some point in their careers. In the 1980s and 1990s, Mike Shanahan was a longtime coach with the Denver Broncos, Los Angeles Raiders and San Francisco 49ers. Especially with the 49ers and QB Steve Young and with the Broncos and QB John Elway, he coached top offenses and won a total of three Super Bowl rings (two as head coach of the Broncos, one as offensive coordinator of the 49ers). Probably the best-known name in his coaching tree today is his son Kyle Shanahan, whose first stops were with other coaches but who keeps referring to his father's philosophy when he explains certain details. The Shanahan coaching tree drew a lot of attention at the end of 2024, when sportswriter Michael Silver (formerly of the San Francisco Chronicle, now at The Athletic) published a book devoted entirely to the subject. That book, "The Why Is Everything," was also the hook and the spark for this series, which takes a closer look at the term "Shanahan scheme."

- **First quarter: Kyle Shanahan's career**
- Second quarter: the origins of the offense and the basics
- Third quarter: what is "scheme"?
- Fourth quarter: Shanahan and his quarterbacks
- Overtime: criticism and conclusion (last section of the fourth quarter)

## First quarter: Kyle Shanahan's career

## First steps as an assistant

Kyle Michael Shanahan was born on December 14, 1979, in Minneapolis, while his father was offensive coordinator at the University of Minnesota, the Golden Gophers. He then grew up with his mother Peggy and his sister Krystal in Colorado, where his father spent most of his coaching career. After one year at Duke University, he transferred to the University of Texas in Austin as a wide receiver. With the Longhorns, however, it soon became clear that his talent as a player would not be enough for the NFL. But even back then, he showed the analytical instinct and the thirst for knowledge that a coach needs in the NFL: "I studied every potential Xs and Os play and issue possible. I spent my whole life working on that. My goal was that any question a player could have about anything on the field, I'd be able to answer it." (Kyle Shanahan, 2006) Kyle Shanahan's first NFL coaching job was as an offensive quality control coach with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers on the staff of Super Bowl winner Jon Gruden. His central task for Gruden was to turn the plays from tape study into diagrams and format them for the playbook. Other well-known coaches on that staff included the legendary Monte Kiffin as DC, John Shoop (QB coach, currently coaching in the ELF), Mike Tomlin (DBs, now Steelers HC), Raheem Morris (assistant DBs, now Falcons HC) and Rich Bisaccia (special teams coordinator, now Packers). After that, Kyle Shanahan went to the Houston Texans as wide receivers coach, where Gary Kubiak, a longtime companion of his father Mike Shanahan, had been hired as head coach. Already on that staff were Mike McDaniel, Johnny Holland, Robert Saleh and Richard Hightower, all of whom would later turn up on the 49ers' staff as well. After one year as QB coach, Shanahan was promoted to offensive coordinator of the Texans in 2008. A new addition to the staff back then was Matt LaFleur, another future NFL head coach. In his second year as play-caller, Shanahan's offense reached its first peak, when QB Matt Schaub finished the season with a league-best 4,770 yards and the passing offense was the No. 1 in the NFL overall.

## From father-son duo to head coach

In 2010, Kyle Shanahan followed his father's call to Washington, where Mike had become head coach of the franchise, then still called the Redskins. Kyle was again named offensive coordinator and also brought Matt LaFleur (QB coach) with him from Houston to the capital. Already on the staff back then were other names well known today, such as Bobby Turner (RB coach), Jon Embree (TE coach), Chris Foerster (offensive line), Sean McVay (offensive assistant) and Richard Hightower (special teams coordinator). Incidentally, the first draft pick of the new Shanahan regime was Trent Williams, selected fourth overall. In 2011, Mike McDaniel followed to the Redskins, while Bobby Slowik, later the Texans' offensive coordinator, had his first contact with the Shanahan system. From today's perspective, four current head coaches (Kyle Shanahan, Sean McVay, Matt LaFleur and Mike McDaniel) were jointly responsible for the Redskins' offense back then. In the third round, the team also picked wide receiver Leonard Hankerson, who now coaches the 49ers' receivers. 2012 was the next highlight year for Shanahan, who, working above all with McDaniel, designed a revolutionary offense for quarterback Robert Griffin III, picked second overall after a blockbuster trade. In the zone-read offense, in which he played mostly out of the pistol formation, "RGIII" ran for more than 800 yards and in the end was even named Rookie of the Year ahead of Andrew Luck, the first overall pick. In his book, Mike Silver mentions the curious story that after the season, both Shanahans believed the success of this offense with RGIII at quarterback could not be sustained, and that the team should therefore try to trade him for high picks, even though he had suffered a severe knee injury in the last playoff game, and go with Kirk Cousins, also drafted in 2012 (fourth round), at quarterback instead. However, then-Redskins owner Dan Snyder insisted that RGIII was the new face of the franchise. In hindsight, it is clear that the Shanahans were not wrong in their assessment. After the 2013 season, Snyder fired Mike Shanahan and many of his assistants. Kyle Shanahan and Mike McDaniel went to the Browns, who would draft Johnny Manziel shortly afterwards, and Matt LaFleur went to the University of Notre Dame, while McVay and Morris were kept on in Washington by new coach Jay Gruden. After a rather disappointing 2014, Shanahan wanted to leave the Browns, already a scandal-ridden franchise at the time, as quickly as possible, and managed to get permission to move to the Atlanta Falcons, where he called the plays for Matt Ryan as offensive coordinator on Dan Quinn's staff. Besides McDaniel, Morris, Matt LaFleur and his brother Mike LaFleur were there again as well. After difficulties in the first season, especially in the coordination between Ryan and Shanahan, the Falcons' offense around Ryan, Julio Jones and Devonta Freeman exploded completely in the 2016 season. Matt Ryan was ultimately named Most Valuable Player, and in the legendary Super Bowl the Falcons lost in overtime to Tom Brady's New England Patriots after leading 28-3. Shanahan was still honored as **Assistant Coach of the Year** and was already talking with several interested teams during the playoffs, above all the San Francisco 49ers and the freshly relocated Los Angeles Rams. The day after the Super Bowl, he was introduced as head coach of the 49ers, after he and Jed York had also agreed during the hiring process that John Lynch would be hired as general manager at the same time. Kyle Shanahan's first 49ers staff in 2017 included many names already mentioned or still familiar today, such as Jon Embree (assistant HC), Mike McDaniel (run game specialist), Bobby Turner (RB), Mike LaFleur (pass game specialist), Robert Saleh (DC), Johnny Holland (LB), Jeff Hafley (DBs, now Packers DC), Richard Hightower (special teams coordinator) and DeMeco Ryans and Bobby Slowik as defensive quality control assistants. Overall, this gives Kyle Shanahan the following coaching record:

![Kyle Shanahan's coaching record](https://i0.wp.com/theninerempiregermany.de/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/Shanahan-Bilanz-1.png?resize=705%2C397&ssl=1)

Source: [https://www.pro-football-reference.com/coaches/ShanKy0.html](https://www.pro-football-reference.com/coaches/ShanKy0.html)

So much for Kyle Shanahan's career. What the special "scheme" is all about, and its roots, which go back to another 49ers legend, you can read in part 2, second quarter: the origins of the offense and the basics.
